name: Icelandic
family: Indo-European, Germanic, North Germanic, West Scandinavian (Insular)
variety: Standard Icelandic in the majority (southern and Reykjavík) pronunciation, with unaspirated stops after vowels and voiceless sonorants before p, t, k; the northern 'hard' pronunciation is noted
sources: Árnason, Kristján (2011). The Phonology of Icelandic and Faroese. Oxford University Press.
Thráinsson, Höskuldur (1994). Icelandic. In König and van der Auwera (eds.), The Germanic Languages. London: Routledge.
Thráinsson, Höskuldur (1978). On the phonology of Icelandic preaspiration. Nordic Journal of Linguistics 1, 3-54.
Helgason, Pétur (2002). Preaspiration in the Nordic Languages: Synchronic and Diachronic Aspects. Doctoral dissertation, Stockholm University.
Garnes, Sara (1976). Quantity in Icelandic: Production and Perception. Hamburg: Buske.
Pétursson, Magnús (1974). Les articulations de l'islandais à la lumière de la radiocinématographie. Paris: Klincksieck.
Einarsson, Stefán (1945). Icelandic: Grammar, Texts, Glossary. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins Press.
Flego, Stefon and Berkson, Kelly (2020). A phonetic illustration of the sound system of Icelandic. Indiana University Linguistics Club Working Papers 20(1).
Dehé, Nicole (2009). An intonational grammar for Icelandic. Nordic Journal of Linguistics 32(1), 5-34.
Dehé, Nicole and Braun, Bettina (2020). The intonation of information-seeking and rhetorical questions in Icelandic. Journal of Germanic Linguistics 32(1).
contrasts: aspirated versus unaspirated stops at the start of a word, all voiceless (tala versus dala, panna versus banna, kala versus gala); there are no voiced stops
preaspirated stops versus plain long stops after a short vowel (hattur [ˈhaʰtʏr] 'hat' versus haddur [ˈhatːʏr] 'hair')
voiced versus voiceless sonorants at the start of a word (l versus hl, n versus hn, r versus hr: lið versus hlið)
palatal versus velar stops before back and front rounded vowels (kjör versus kör, gjóla versus góla)
long versus short consonants after a short vowel (vina versus vinna, which also differ in vowel length)
eight monophthongs and five diphthongs, all of which occur long and short by position
/θ/ and /ð/, in complementary distribution by position in the word
allophony: pp, tt, kk are preaspirated [ʰp ʰt ʰk], and so are p, t, k before l and n: epli [ˈɛʰplɪ], vatn [vaʰtn̥], opna [ˈɔʰpna], þakka [ˈθaʰka]; the preaspiration takes the time of a full segment

sonorants are voiceless before p, t, k in the majority pronunciation: lampi [ˈlam̥pɪ], vanta [ˈvan̥ta], banki [ˈpauɲ̊cɪ], mjólk [mjoul̥k], hjálpa, verk; in the northern pronunciation the sonorant stays voiced and the stop is aspirated
hl, hn, hr at the start of a word are voiceless sonorants [l̥ n̥ r̥]; hj is [ç] (hjarta); hv is [kʰv], in the south-east [xv]
p, t, k after a vowel are unaspirated [p t k] in the majority pronunciation (tapa [ˈtʰaːpa], vita, taka) and aspirated in the north
ll is [tl] and nn after an accented vowel or diphthong is [tn] (allur [ˈatlʏr], fjall [fjatl̥], seinn [seitn̥], steinn); rl and rn are [(r)tl] and [(r)tn] (karl, barn [pa(r)tn̥])
sonorants and /ð/ are devoiced at the end of a word before a pause (dalur, það)

g is a stop [k] at the start of a word, after a consonant and when doubled, a fricative [ɣ] between a vowel and a, u, ð, r (saga [ˈsaːɣa]), [x] before t and s (lagt [laxt]), [j] between a vowel and i or j (segja, stigi), and it is lost between á, ó, ú and a following a or u (fljúga)
k and g before front vowels and j are palatal [cʰ c] (keyra, gefa, gæs)
f is [v] between vowels and at the end of a word after a vowel (hafa), [p] before l and n (Keflavík, höfn [hœpn̥])
vowels before ng and nk are changed: a is [au], e is [ei], ö is [œi], i and y are [i], u is [u] (langur [ˈlauŋkʏr], banki)

stressed vowels and diphthongs are long in open syllables: at the end of a word, before a single consonant, and before p, t, k, s followed by v, j, r (tala, vita, nepja, vökva, Esja, titra); they are short before other clusters and before long or preaspirated consonants
/r/ is an alveolar trill or tap; /s/ is always voiceless
a linking vowel u [ʏ] appears in endings (-ur), which keeps final clusters simple
phonotactics: stress is always on the first syllable, so every word begins with a stressed syllable
a stressed syllable is heavy: long vowel, or short vowel plus long consonant or cluster
unstressed syllables of native words have only /ɪ a ʏ/, without centralisation
there are no voiced stops and no voiced sibilant
voiceless sonorants occur at the start of a word, before p, t, k and before a pause
[θ] stands at the start of a word or stem and [ð] elsewhere
onset clusters of up to three consonants (str, skr, spj, stj)

stress.rule: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of every word; secondary stress falls on the first syllable of later members of a compound and otherwise on alternate syllables.
stress.cues: duration of the stressed rhyme (long vowel or long consonant), pitch movement when accented, and intensity; vowel quality plays no part

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none: unstressed vowels keep their quality, but only /ɪ a ʏ/ occur in endings
rhythm.notes: Trochaic rhythm with fixed initial stress and heavy stressed syllables, but no vowel reduction. I know of no instrumental rhythm classification that I can cite.

length.notes: Vowel length is decided by syllable structure and is not contrastive by itself; consonant length and preaspiration carry the contrast (vina [ˈvɪːna] versus vinna [ˈvɪnːa]). Garnes (1976) is the classic duration study; I cannot quote its figures with confidence.

intonation.declarative: rising or high accents on the stressed syllables of accented words, a falling nuclear accent on the last accented word, downstep through the utterance, and a low boundary
intonation.yes_no_question: verb-first word order marks the question; the nuclear accent is a late rise (L*+H), and the utterance still ends in a fall to a low boundary
intonation.wh_question: high start and a peak accent (H*) on or after the question word, final fall to a low boundary
intonation.continuation: high boundary at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: monotonal H* and bitonal accents of the types L*+H and H*+L, aligned with the word-initial stressed syllable
intonation.notes: After Árnason (2011), Dehé (2009) and Dehé and Braun (2020), who report that contours of all sentence types typically end in a final fall.

tone.notes: Icelandic has no word accents of the Swedish and Norwegian kind.

phonation: preaspiration: a period of voiceless glottal friction between a short vowel and a following stop
voiceless sonorants (nasals, laterals and trills), partly with friction
postaspiration of initial /pʰ tʰ cʰ kʰ/

problems: the long vowels E: and W: ([ɛː] and [œː]) have the same length value as the short vowels (130), while the other long vowels have 230, so gefa, vera and similar words have no long vowel
yes-no questions get the generic question tune with a final rise; Icelandic questions end in a fall after a late-rising nuclear accent

nn after a long vowel or diphthong at the end of a word gives a stop plus a voiced [n] (seinn, steinn), where the language has a voiceless [tn̥]; devoicing before a pause is written into the rules for l, ll and gn only
the rules for r insert extra segments: keyra comes out with a tap followed by a trill, ískra with a schwa before the r
the voiceless sonorants have IPA names that are not IPA (n#, l#, r#, m#), so the phoneme trace cannot be read by IPA tools; the voiceless nasals carry the attribute 'voiced' in the phoneme table
preaspiration is a plain [h] phoneme before an unaspirated stop; its length relative to the stop closure is not controlled
the pronunciation list has about 330 entries, so loans, names and irregular words are read by the letter rules (ll is always [tl], also in loans and pet names)
only the majority pronunciation is available; there is no setting for the northern one
good: preaspiration is produced for pp, tt, kk and for p, t, k before l and n (epli, vatn, opna, þakka)
voiceless sonorants are produced at the start of a word (hl, hn, hr) and before p, t, k (lampi, vanta, banki, mjólk)
ll, nn, rl and rn get their stop onsets (allur, fjall, barn)
all stops are voiceless, medial p, t, k are unaspirated, and k, g are palatal before front vowels
g and f have their fricative and stop allophones by position (saga, lagt, segja, hafa, hafði)
vowel length follows the syllable structure rule, and stress is initial

notes: The consonant list is phonetic, because the distribution of aspiration and voicelessness is what a synthesiser must produce; phonemic analyses are smaller. The long vowels in the vowel list are positional variants of the short ones. The diphthongs ɔi and ʏi arise before gi (bogi, hugi). I give no formant, duration or voice onset time values because I cannot quote the published figures with confidence.
